description: Take the Arc de Triomphe apart piece by piece in 3D, and read the story of Napoleon's arch: thirty years a-building, a biplane through the vault, and the Unknown Soldier beneath.

intro: It took thirty years to build, survived every regime that followed the one that ordered it, and once had a biplane flown through it. The Arc de Triomphe is Napoleon's monument that outlived Napoleon and became, instead, the monument of France itself.

sections.body: After his victory at Austerlitz in 1805, Napoleon decreed a triumphal arch for the armies of France. Jean Chalgrin designed it in 1806 on the Roman model of the Arch of Titus, but at a scale Rome never attempted: 50 metres high, 45 wide and 22 deep, without columns. Chalgrin died before it rose far; Goust, Huyot and Blouet carried it on, and Louis-Philippe inaugurated it in 1836, dedicating it to the Armies of the Revolution and the Empire.
sections.heading: Thirty years a-building

sections.body: The arch honours those who fought and died for France in the Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars. Its inner and outer faces carry the names of French victories and 660 individuals, 558 of them generals. Four colossal sculpture groups flank the piers; the greatest is Francois Rude's La Marseillaise, the Departure of the Volunteers of 1792, on the Champs-Elysees face. Thirty shields ring the attic. The great vault runs 29.19 metres high and 14.62 wide; the transverse vaults 18.68 by 8.44.
sections.heading: Names in stone

sections.body: In 1921 the body of an unknown French soldier of the First World War was buried beneath the vault, and in 1923 the eternal flame was lit. It has been rekindled every evening at 6:30 pm since, interrupted only by the German occupation. The tomb made the arch the ceremonial heart of the republic: victory parades, state funerals and the 14 July military parade all pass through the Place Charles de Gaulle, where twelve avenues meet.
sections.heading: The Unknown Soldier

sections.body: The arch sits at the centre of the Axe historique, the grand line from the Louvre courtyard to the Grande Arche de La Defense. Three weeks after the 1919 victory parade, aviator Charles Godefroy flew his Nieuport biplane straight through the great vault, on newsreel. In 2021 Christo's estate wrapped the entire monument in silvery fabric for sixteen days, L'Arc de Triomphe, Wrapped, a project the artist had imagined since the 1960s. The Lumiere brothers had filmed the arch as early as 1896.
sections.heading: In the cultural conversation

sections.body: Cinema keeps coming back to the roundabout. Richard Linklater's Before Sunset (2004) walks its lovers under the arch and across the empty boulevard at dusk. John Wick: Chapter 4 (2023) staged a full battle in the traffic around it; director Chad Stahelski called the sequence a stress attack, since the production could not simply close one of Europe's busiest roundabouts and had to choreograph stunt drivers, henchmen and dogs through live traffic. No film has yet topped Godefroy: fiction has never flown anything through the vault for real.
sections.heading: The movies circle it

timeline.text: Napoleon decrees the arch after Austerlitz; Chalgrin designs it on the Arch of Titus.
Inaugurated by Louis-Philippe, dedicated to the Armies of the Revolution and the Empire.
Charles Godefroy flies his Nieuport biplane through the great vault.
The Unknown Soldier is interred beneath the vault; the eternal flame follows in 1923.
Christo's L'Arc de Triomphe, Wrapped covers the monument for sixteen days.
